newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's crisis caused by capital outflow - report.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's crisis caused by capital outflow - report.

text.p: Bulgaria's parliament committee against corruption on Thursday blamed the country's current grave financial crisis on uncontrolled siphoning of funds abroad through banks, brokerages and other companies.

"At a time when the government is struggling to win a $100 million IMF tranche, more than $100 million was exported abroad this year in banknotes by several private and state banks," committee deputy chairman Edwin Sugarev told a news conference presenting a White Paper on bank bankruptcies.

Bulgaria's payments due next year consist of $1.2 billion on foreign debt, a total of 598.5 billion levs in maturing government securities and a further 80 billion levs due as compensation payments on personal and company deposits in 12 banks for which the government is seeking insolvency orders.

"These obligations are matched by a $540 million central bank reserve, a plundered, agonizing banking system, a stagnant economy, and an ageing population half of which relies on pensions or social benefits," said Sugarev.
He said an International Monetary Fund proposal to introduce a currency board was an acknowledgement "that Bulgaria has neither the resources nor the chances to recover alone".
Currency boards, usually pegging the local currency to the dollar have been used to defeat hyperinflation and restore confidence in countries like Argentina, Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia.
The IMF and other multilateral lenders have said corruption has deterred urgent economic reforms in the past seven years since the collapse of communist rule.
Sugarev, an opposition deputy, said Bulgaria's banking system was set up less to service the real economy than to cater to its founders' business interests.
"The luxurious offices and cars and the clerks are the only thing left of Bulgaria's banks," said Sugarev.
He said the banking system had been used to translate leading former communists' political power into economic power.
Sugarev accused bankers of deliberate mismanagement by extending uncollateralised credits which were never collected, giving preference to banks' shareholding companies.
Quoting bank documents, Sugarev cited the Atlantida company, which used 2.5 million live fish in a reservoir as collateral for a $4 million credit from Sirbank, which merged with other banks in 1995.
He said the central bank provided generous refinancing to commercial banks, which they in turn transfered to parallel institutions like brokerage houses and siphoned abroad.

In the first six months of this year nine state owned and private banks have mailed abroad 2,811 kg in dispatches registered as valuable at Sofia airport customs, he said, quoting a classified Interior Ministry report.
The report added that $1 million in $100 bills weighs 8 kg.

An additional burden on the economy is Bulgaria's 650 billion lev domestic debt, half of which was accrued through massive issues of government securities to cover an ever increasing budget deficit created in the past two years of Socialist rule, said the white paper.

The currency board, under which the amount of national currency in circulation must be exactly matched by the central bank's hard currency reserves, would succeed in Bulgaria only with substantial external support, said Sugarev.
